summary: Updates RFC 6775, 6LoWPAN Neighbor Discovery, to clarify its role as a registration technique and simplify registration in 6LoWPAN routers. It also adds registration capabilities and mobility enhancements.

eli5.summary: Little devices sign in with a nearby router so it knows where they are. This makes sign-in simpler and works if they move.

subtitle: Reworks 6LoWPAN Neighbor Discovery so low-power nodes can register addresses simply, safely and while moving.

tldr.problem: RFC 6775 gave low-power IPv6 networks an address registration mechanism, but it was tied to MAC-derived identifiers, could not tell which of two registrations was newer for a moving node, and was heavy for routers handling link-local addresses.
tldr.mechanism: The Extended Address Registration Option (EARO) adds a Transaction ID counter, a flexible Registration Ownership Verifier, an R flag for routing or proxy service and new status codes, and link-local addresses no longer need duplicate-address exchanges with the border router.
tldr.outcome: Registration becomes a general technique that supports mobility, proxy registration and privacy addresses, and updated nodes stay backward compatible with RFC 6775-only devices. RFC 8505 is a Proposed Standard that has itself been updated.

today: RFC 8505 is a Proposed Standard and updates RFC 6775. It has not been obsoleted, but it is itself updated by RFC 8928, RFC 8929, RFC 9010, RFC 9685 and RFC 9926.

sections.title: What RFC 8505 Changes
sections.content:
IPv6 Low-Power and Lossy Networks (LLNs) can be stars or meshes. For them, RFC 6775 (6LoWPAN Neighbor Discovery) defines a registration mechanism and a central IPv6 ND Registrar so that addresses are unique, and it reduces reliance on network-layer multicast and link-layer broadcast. RFC 8505 updates that document to simplify and generalize registration in 6LoWPAN Routers (6LRs).

It lets a network determine the most recent location of a mobile node, simplifies registration for link-local addresses, supports routing-unaware leaf nodes in a route-over network, allows proxy registration, adds a way to verify ownership of a registration (the ROVR), allows registration to an IPv6 ND proxy such as a Routing Registrar, and gives better support for privacy and temporary addresses.

The registration is treated as a technique in its own right. A router that serves it needs enough storage for the Neighbor Cache Entries of all the addresses that may be registered to it, whether or not they are actively communicating, and the vendor MUST document how many registrations are supported.
sections.eli5: Think of a school where every kid tells the hall monitor which classroom they are in. This update makes that check-in easier and keeps it correct even when kids move around.

sections.title: The Cast of Nodes
sections.content:
A 6LN is a 6LoWPAN node, often a host. A 6LR is a 6LoWPAN router that accepts its registrations, and a 6LBR is the 6LoWPAN border router that keeps a registry for the whole domain. The Registered Node owns the address, and the Registering Node performs the registration, which is either the same node or a proxy acting for it.

An IPv6 ND Registrar processes a registration and answers with an NA or EDAC message carrying the EARO and a status. A Routing Registrar goes further and provides reachability services for the Registered Address, such as duplicate address detection and proxy NA. A Backbone Router (6BBR) is a Routing Registrar that proxies these operations so that several LLNs joined by a backbone link behave as a single IPv6 subnet.

An implementation or message that follows only RFC 6775 is called "RFC 6775-only", and one that supports RFC 8505 is called "updated".
sections.eli5: Some gadgets are visitors, some are helpers who write down who is here, and one is the head helper who keeps the main list for the whole building.

sections.title: The EARO and Extended Messages
sections.content:
The RFC introduces no new options. It modifies existing ones. The Extended Address Registration Option (EARO, option type 33) reworks the ARO from RFC 6775. Its fields include a Status (0 in a Neighbor Solicitation), an Opaque octet, a 2-bit I field, an R flag, a T flag, a one-byte Transaction ID (TID), a 16-bit Registration Lifetime in minutes and the Registration Ownership Verifier (ROVR). The old EUI-64 field becomes the ROVR, which is 64 bits when backward compatibility is needed and may be 128, 192 or 256 bits otherwise.

The R flag asks a Routing Registrar to ensure reachability for the address, for example by routing or proxy ND. A registration lifetime of 0 means the registration has ended and its state MUST be removed. When registering, a node that is only a host MUST set R.

The Duplicate Address Request and Confirmation messages are extended into EDAR and EDAC, carrying the same TID and ROVR across the mesh. A non-null Code Suffix signals support, with values 1 to 4 meaning ROVR sizes of 64, 128, 192 and 256 bits. The 6LoWPAN Capability Indication Option (6CIO, type 36) gains the bits D, L, B, P and E so routers can advertise what they support.

New status codes tell a node why a registration failed, among them 3 (Moved), 4 (Removed), 5 (Validation Requested), 8 (Registered Address Topologically Incorrect), 9 (6LBR Registry Saturated) and 10 (Validation Failed).
sections.eli5: The sign-in form gets a few new boxes: a counter that says how new this sign-in is, a secret stamp that proves who you are, and a note for why a sign-in was refused.

sections.title: Tracking Moves and Ownership
sections.content:
The Transaction ID is a sequence number that the node increments with each re-registration. The network uses the most recent TID to find where a moving node now is. When the node registers to several 6LRs in parallel it MUST use the same TID, so that registrars can tell identical registrations from a movement. The TID behaves like the RPL Path Sequence counter and uses a "lollipop" scheme: values from 128 up form a linear sequence that marks a restart, and values up to 127 form a circular space of size 128. Two values further apart than SEQUENCE_WINDOW (16) are not comparable, and the node should then prefer the more recently incremented one.

The ROVR correlates repeated attempts to register the same IPv6 address, so only the original owner can update a registration. It can be a unique identifier such as an EUI-64 or a cryptographic token. Its scope is a single address, and it MUST NOT be used to correlate registrations of different addresses. A node SHOULD keep the ROVR, or enough to regenerate it, in persistent memory, or it may be unable to re-register after a reboot until the old state times out.
sections.eli5: Each time you check in, you write a bigger number on your ticket, so the helpers know which ticket is the newest if you changed rooms. Your secret stamp proves the ticket is really yours.

sections.title: Registering and Maintaining State
sections.content:
In the updated flow, the address being registered goes in the Target Address of the NS(EARO) instead of the Source Address. A registration is an NS(EARO) that also carries a Source Link-Layer Address option. This lets a proxy register on behalf of another node, for example a 6LBR registering with a Routing Registrar.

Link-local addresses are simplified. They only need to be unique from the point of view of the two nodes that use them, so the 6LR can answer right away and the EDAR/EDAC exchange with the 6LBR is skipped for them. A node MUST use a link-local address as the source of its registration. A node with no registered address registers a link-local one first, using it as both source and target.

To keep state accurate, a node renews by sending a new NS(EARO), and a node that stops using an address SHOULD de-register it with a lifetime of 0. A node that moves SHOULD de-register at the old 6LR and register at the new one with an incremented TID, and the old location is cleaned up using a "Moved" status. If a 6LR is out of space it answers with status 2 (Neighbor Cache Full) and the node may try another 6LR. If the 6LBR registry is full, the 6LBR returns "6LBR Registry Saturated", which is network-wide, so another 6LR will not help.
sections.eli5: When you move to a new classroom you tell the new monitor, and the old classroom gets told you have left. If a classroom is full, you can try the next one, but if the whole school is full, you have to wait.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
An updated node can coexist with RFC 6775-only devices. A 6LN that talks to a 6LR not known to support the update MUST behave in a backward compatible way, and one that finds updated support MUST follow the new rules. An updated 6LN always uses the EARO in place of the ARO, which works because the new T flag and TID occupy fields that were reserved and ignored by older routers.

Routers announce support through the 6CIO in Router Advertisements; if no 6CIO is present, the 6LR is assumed to be RFC 6775-only. With such a router the ROVR MUST be 64 bits. An updated 6LR MUST accept a valid RFC 6775-style registration and uses the RFC 6775 DAR and DAC messages toward the 6LBR. If the 6LBR is RFC 6775-only, the 6LR uses only the leftmost 64 bits of the ROVR in the EDAR message.

Letting an RFC 6775-only DAR update state created by the updated protocol would be an attack vector, so that is not the default behavior.
sections.eli5: New check-in forms still work with old monitors, because the new boxes sit in spots the old monitors skip over.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
RFC 6775 does not protect its message contents and relies on lower-layer encryption. RFC 8505 requires the LLN MAC layer to provide secure unicast to and from a Routing Registrar and secure broadcast or multicast from it, in a way that prevents tampering with or replaying the ND messages. A trust model MUST ensure only authorized devices act as 6LBR or Routing Registrar, or an impostor could destroy state with the "Removed" status.

A rogue node could try to saturate the registry of a 6LR or 6LBR. The TID helps detect and clean up stale registrations and defeat replay. A router should be configurable to limit the addresses one node can register as a protective measure only, and it MUST be able to keep a minimum number of addresses per node, which ranges from 3 for a very constrained LLN to 10 for a larger device. When the limit is reached, a least-recently-used algorithm should be used, keeping at least one link-local address.

On privacy, the protocol does not limit how many addresses a device may form, and it discourages building the link-local interface identifier from EUI-64 because that blocks address privacy techniques.
sections.eli5: The school only lets trusted helpers keep the list, because a fake helper could erase everyone. Each kid can hold a few names, so one kid cannot use up all the spots.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Option length in units of 8 bytes.

fields.name: Status
fields.desc: Registration result in an NA; MUST be 0 in an NS.

fields.name: Opaque
fields.desc: Octet opaque to ND; MUST be 0 when not used.

fields.name: I
fields.desc: Type of the Opaque field; 0 means topology index.

fields.name: R
fields.desc: Requests reachability services from a Routing Registrar.

fields.name: T
fields.desc: Set when the TID field is used.

fields.name: ROVR
fields.desc: Registration Ownership Verifier; 64 bits when backward compatible, longer sizes otherwise.

messages.label: Extended DAR
messages.note: Relays the registration across the mesh.

messages.label: proxy NS(EARO)
messages.note: Registers for reachability; the registrar injects a host route or proxy ND state.

messages.label: NA(EARO)
messages.note: Carries the status of the registration.

items.label: Moved
items.desc: A more recent registration exists, as shown by the same ROVR and a newer TID.

items.label: Validation Requested
items.desc: The registering node is challenged to prove ownership or proxy rights.

items.label: Duplicate Source Address
items.desc: The NS source address conflicts with an existing registration.

items.label: Invalid Source Address
items.desc: The NS source address is not a link-local address.

items.label: Registered Address Topologically Incorrect
items.desc: The address is not usable on this link.

items.label: 6LBR Registry Saturated
items.desc: The 6LBR cannot accept a new registration.

items.label: Validation Failed
items.desc: The proof of ownership is not correct.
